document.title: Comments of Suzanne Glatz and Abraham Silverman in response to PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.'s et al. 03/24/2025 filings

pages.text:
1 
 
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA 
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION 
 
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., et al. 
 
)  Docket Nos. EL25-49-000 
 
 
Large Loads Co-Located at Generating Facilities 
 
 
)  AD24-11-000 
 
Constellation Energy Generation, LLC 
v. 
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. 
)  EL25-20-000 
  (Consolidated) 
 
 
Reply Comments of Suzanne Glatz and Abraham Silverman 
 
 
 
Pursuant to Rules 206 and 213 of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s 
(“Commission”) Rules of Practice and Procedure, 18 C.F.R. § 385.206 .213, and as directed 
by the Commission in Docket No. EL25-49-000, Suzanne Glatz and Abraham Silverman, 
respectfully submits these comments in response to the filings dated March 24, 2025 of PJM 
Interconnection, L.L.C. (“PJM”), and the Indicated PJM Transmission Owners, made in 
response to Commission’s February 20, 2025 Order Instituting Proceeding under Section 206 
of the Federal Power Act and Consolidating with Other Proceedings (the “Show Cause 
Order”).1 
I. 
Summary  
The unprecedented growth in demand in the PJM region driven by large customers, 
primarily data centers, is driving the need for significant new transmission and exasperating 
resource adequacy concerns due, in large part, to an aging generation fleet and long delays in 
interconnecting new generation.  While co-location allows large loads to bypass the 
conventional load connection process and accelerate data center deployment, if not carefully 
managed, co-location also has the potential to push the PJM region into a resource adequacy 
and affordability crisis.  
 
Since the formation of PJM, load customers seeking to connect to the grid have taken 
Network Integration Transmission Service (“NITS”) to connect to the grid.  While the 
 
1 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., et al., 190 FERC ¶ 61,115 (2025).

2 
 
Artificial Intelligence (“AI”) revolution provides an opportunity to discuss improvements to 
PJM’s existing transmission offerings – in particular, through the creation of a curtailable 
service option and increased contract terms for new large NITS customers to protect 
customers against stranded transmission investments – we see the underlying NITS structure 
as fundamentally sound.  Thus, we largely agree with the position advanced by the PJM 
Transmission Owners2 and in PJM’s Existing Option 1 that the existing PJM tariff is just and 
reasonable.34  
Disputes over co-location should not distract from the urgency to actively manage 
load growth and bring more energy resources to the grid.  PJM’s 2025/2026 capacity auction 
procured only 514 megawatts (“MW”) of excess above the Installed Reserve Margin.  PJM 
predicts 2,700 MW of additional load growth for the 2026/2027 delivery year – largely driven 
by data centers.  Whether load is co-located with generation in a “behind-the-generator-meter” 
configuration or in a conventional load connection, the issue remains that PJM must balance 
the amount of new data center load and new generation resources for the system to remain 
reliable and affordable.   
We recognize the interest in co-location and the commercial value of connecting data 
centers on an expedited basis, including allowing generation to directly serve end-use 
customer load.  The current tariff does not contain provisions to specifically describe how a 
generator and a retail load can jointly or separately request to connect to the PJM grid in a co-
location configuration, and recommend that PJM develop: 
• 
A new pro forma interconnection agreement with an accompanying rate structure 
specific to the co-location business model; 
 
• 
A safety valve to ensure that co-located data center load does not plunge PJM into a 
reliability or affordability crisis; 
 
• 
Minimum term requirements for new transmission service requests from large loads, 
backed by financial security requirements;  
 
2 Answer of Indicated PJM Transmission Owners to the Show Cause Order, at p. 10.   
3 Answer of PJM Interconnection to the Show Cause Order, at p. 10.

3 
 
 
• 
A new type of non-firm transmission service that allows for faster connections in 
exchange for operational flexibility; and  
 
• 
Clear regulatory obligations of generators serving on-site customer load.    
 
In these comments we will discuss more specifically why the current Tariff is inadequate to 
accommodate co-location and offer potential models for consideration and further 
development in a transparent and open stakeholder forum. 
II. 
Background of Suzanne Glatz and Abraham Silverman 
These comments are submitted on behalf of Suzanne Glatz and Abraham Silverman.  
These comments are not filed on behalf of any party and represent the personal opinions of 
the authors.   
Suzanne Glatz has worked in the energy industry for close to 40 years in various 
capacities that include many facets of transmission and distribution planning.  Ms. Glatz is 
currently an independent consultant supporting entities navigating the complexity of regional 
planning processes.  Prior to starting her independent consulting business, Ms. Glatz was 
employed by PJM for the period of 2011-2023, where her last position was Director, Strategic 
Initiatives and Interregional Planning.  
Abraham Silverman is a research scholar at Johns Hopkins University’s Ralph 
O’Connor Sustainable Energy Institute and principal of Silvergreen Energy Consulting, LLC.  
Mr. Silverman holds degrees from the University of Maryland the George Washington 
University Law School.  He has worked in the energy industry in a variety of positions, 
including at the Commission, in private law practice, at NRG Energy, Inc., a leading 
independent power producer.  Most recently, he served as General Counsel and Executive 
Policy Counsel at the New Jersey Board of Public Utilities from 2019 to 2023.  Since leaving 
state service, he has been employed as a researcher at Columbia University and Johns 
Hopkins University.

4 
 
III. 
Comments 
 
 
A. PJM’s Existing NITS Rules are Just and Reasonable and Not Unduly 
Discriminatory or Preferential to Co-location Customers.     
 
The existing PJM Tariff unambiguously affords the ability to connect new customers 
in a co-location arrangement, provided the customer load is willing to be treated as network 
load and contributes to the fixed costs of operating the transmission grid through its NITS 
allocation.  While changing needs on the grid certainly leave room for improvements to the 
PJM framework for serving new data center load, it is also important to recognize that the 
existing system provides a stable foundation that permits new load to connect to the grid.  As 
PJM notes,5 the options available to customers today include the ability of a generator to be 
physically co-located with generation.   
Critical to the Commission’s approach is the fact that co-location arrangements can 
occur with a rapidity that our existing planning processes are not designed to address.  While 
existing rules also allow utilities to ensure that new loads are connected in an orderly manner 
and that new service is only allowed to commence once transmission needs have been 
addressed, any accelerated co-location process must address what happens if a co-location 
request would precipitate a resource adequacy or affordability crisis.  This should include 
upfront rules about deadlines for providing advance notice, study processes, and, ideally, an 
opportunity for relevant state agencies to provide feedback.  Any rules coming out of this 
proceeding should continue to prioritize system reliability and affordability and avoid creating 
a situation where data center expansion contributes to a transmission or resource adequacy 
shortfall.  While it is important that PJM and the Commission facilitate access for new users 
of the electric grid, the desire of data center customers for accelerated grid access must be 
balanced against the threat of increased rates and diminished reliability.   
The lost transmission revenue can be significant.  Based on data provided by the 
Indicated Transmission Owners, the potential cost impact to customers by large loads evading 
 
5 Answer of PJM Interconnection LLC, Exhibit A, Summary of Options.

5 
 
grid charges could be on the order of millions of dollars on an annual basis, potentially 
resulting in customer bill increases between 1 to 10 percent, depending on the utility zone.6  
The increase in resource adequacy and energy prices has the potential to be even more 
significant, particularly if data center-driven load growth causes the PJM region to sink below 
its IRM requirements, which puts upward pressure on both capacity and energy costs. 
B. Any Just and Reasonable Changes to PJM’s Tariff Should Ensure that 
Comparable Electrical Impacts Incur Comparable Transmission Charges.  
 
If the Commission elects to direct changes to PJM’s existing tariff methodology for 
assigning transmission charges to co-located load, it should ensure that use-cases with similar 
electrical impacts pay comparable rates.  As we explained in our prior comments, PJM’s 
electrical studies “studies do not generate different results because a load is co-located with 
generation on one side of the breaker versus on the other side as network load.  Electrically, 
the flows are the same.”7 
The corollary to this principle is that what “type” of meter is used to connect a new 
load can have significant implications for cost allocation.  Load located behind a “generator 
meter” pays one rate; load located behind a “load meter” pays a different rate – even though   
the electrical impacts are identical.  Customers located behind a load meter are subject to a 
host of charges that simply do not apply to customers locating behind a generator meter.8  For 
example, generators only pay for “but-for the generator” system upgrades when they go 
through the initial interconnection cost allocation process and are categorically exempt from 
transmission service, ancillary service, and Schedule 12 Regional Transmission Expansion 
Planning (“RTEP”) baseline upgrade costs.  If any new (i.e., post-interconnection) upgrades 
are required to maintain a reliable grid and comply with mandatory NERC standards, 
generators will not be assigned cost responsibility.  This is true even if the generator retires, in 
 
6 Answer of the PJM Indicated Transmission Owners, at p. 19. 
7 Post-Technical Conference Comments of Suzanne Glatz and Abraham Silverman, at p. 5. 
8 The differing rate treatment between “generator meters” and “load meters” also helps explain why 
traditional combined heat and power facilities have not triggered the same concern.  There, the co-
generation facility is typically located behind a load meter.

6 
 
part or in entirety.  RTEP upgrade costs are likewise paid for solely by network load 
customers.   
Assigning all transmission costs to network load is a reasonable method of assigning 
costs when all generation serves load connected to the grid and is subject to the same rates.  
Otherwise, connected load under a rate that is applicable to a generator will result in the load 
not paying its fair share of the cost of operating the transmission grid and leading to 
preferential treatment to co-located load and potentially free ridership on the grid.  
C. Principles for a New Interconnection Service if FERC Determines that 
Alternative Tariff Rules are Required. 
 
One of the key questions facing the Commission in this docket (assuming it elects to 
take action) is whether generators that have gone through the existing PJM interconnection 
process need to be re-analyzed when adding co-located load, and if so, what that study should 
look like.  As a guiding principle, we recommend that the Commission adopt a principle of 
“comparability” designed to ensure that new co-location arrangements go through a study 
process that is comparable in terms of timing and cost responsibility to a new load locating in-
front-of-the-meter.  Such an approach would help the “regulatory gap”9 between the generator 
interconnection process and the Commission’s prior holding in Order No. 2003-A that 
“Interconnection Service is separate from the delivery component of Transmission Service.”10      
In its answer, PJM identified five options as new options that are not currently available to 
customers without revisions to the tariff.  These options all fall short of achieving the type of 
comparability between co-located and front-of-the-meter customers that we advocate.  We are 
concerned that an appropriate set of studies should recognize all potential modes of operation 
– both generation and load – and be studied appropriately, including addressing what happens 
 
9 See Post-Technical Conference Comments of Suzanne Glatz and Abraham Silverman in Docket No. 
AD24-11-000, Page 6 (“It is difficult (if not impossible) to harmonize the concept of connecting new 
network load behind the meter of an existing generation facilities with the Commission’s directive that 
generator interconnection service is “not the same as, or a substitute for” NITS.  The end result is a gap 
in how transmission providers are studying and assigning cost responsibility for load collocated with 
generation.”) 
10 Order No. 2003-A at P 113 (capitalization in original).

7 
 
if a generator elects to effectively remove itself from the grid as part of a co-location 
arrangement.   
For example, PJM Options 4, 5, 7 and 8 all raise significant transparency issues 
around whether the studies PJM would carry out are comparable to the studies normally 
carried out both as part of a large load interconnection process and the generator 
interconnection process.  PJM states “that any configuration where the co-located load is 
Network Load (Options 2, 3, 7, and 8, and in some circumstances Options 4 and 5) is limited 
in scope to generator interconnection modifications [and] Transmission Owner retail load 
integration studies would be performed in addition to necessary studies.”11  However, we 
have significant concerns that the PJM Necessary Study Process would not be suitable for the 
addition of retail/end-use load, only for “...modifications to its facilities.”12  To accommodate 
this new business model, it may be determined that with suitable revisions to the Tariff, the 
Necessary Study may be applicable under certain conditions, but should not be used as a 
matter of course due to, among other things, its lack of transparency.   
Our concerns with the lack of transparency associated with the Necessary Study 
process is underscored by the response from the PJM Indicated Transmission Owners which 
identifies the need for “the necessary study process, together with other studies and analysis, 
which include the individual TO’s feasibility/engineering studies[.]”13  However, these 
additional studies and analyses are not clearly spelled out, nor is there any transparency for 
consumers.  Further, we continue to question whether the necessary study process is 
 
11 Answer of PJM to the Show Cause Order, at p. 8. 
12 See PJM Tariff, Section Appendix 2, Standard Terms and Conditions, para 3.1 specifies that the 
Necessary Study is intended to address modifications to its facilities, “[i]ncluding any modification to 
its project that causes the project’s capacity, location, configuration or technology to differ from any 
corresponding information provided in the Interconnection Request.”  The Necessary Study provisions 
do not specify changes to or modifications to customer load and Tariff changes should implemented to 
specify the conditions when such a study might be suitable and when it is not, comparable to the 
provisions that detail changes to the generator facilities. 
13 Answer of the PJM Indicated Transmission Owners, at Attachment A, p. 12.

8 
 
appropriate for understanding the impacts of a generator that is, effectively, electing to 
remove a portion, or all, of its generating capacity from the PJM markets.14   
A reduction in Capacity Injection Rights (“CIRs”) is effectively a partial deactivation.  
To suggest a reduction of 300 MW of capacity does not warrant a deactivation study when a 
full deactivation of a 20 MW generator does, appears illogical on its face.  The generator will 
not have the obligation to offer in those CIRs, whether due to a reduction or a full retirement.  
Any change in available capacity will impact markets and transmission flows.  The system 
capacity that is made available by a reduction in CIRs could potentially benefit all system 
users but is not made available if it is studied in concert with a behind-the-meter discrete load 
addition.  When CIRs are removed from the system, the existing load must still be served and 
the generation to serve that load may require new network upgrades.  Further, without a 
deactivation study, it is unclear how the market monitor can be effective in providing 
independent oversight of PJM markets and operations when such CIR reductions can be 
affecting market outcomes. Evaluating such changes in CIRs without a deactivation study 
through an opaque necessary study process appears to be a means to avoiding review by the 
Market Monitor.   
Additionally, the majority of PJM’s proposed options aim at facilitating co-location 
of load at existing generators that already have an interconnection agreement, rather than 
focusing on the development of sorely needed new generation to serve the new loads.  Option 
6 includes new generation with the load and suggests “faster interconnection when load is 
network load,” but it is unclear how this would be accomplished any faster than the current 
interconnection queue.  Nor is it clear why Option 6 should provide large load customers a 
 
14 The Indicated Transmission Owner’s Answer suggests that PJM is effectively powerless to 
address any loss of generator capacity associated with co-location, suggesting that “PJM’s 
role should be limited to the standard transmission planning process for all new load additions” 
and that “the loss of capacity from an existing generator seeking to enter into a co-location 
arrangement should be studied by PJM.  Because the federal role in end-use load additions is 
limited, PJM and the Commission should not create processes in the PJM Tariff that would 
interfere with state jurisdiction.”  Answer of PJM Indicated Transmission Owners, at 
Appendix A, p. 12.

9 
 
preference in interconnection over customers who are looking to meet other energy objectives, 
including clean energy commitments.   
One option would be a four-party agreement among the co-located generator, co-
located load, interconnecting transmission owner, and PJM.  A new pro forma process would 
entail the following steps: 
1. 
Establish new customer categories: Co-located Generator and Co-located Load, 
where the generator and the load parties would be eligible to interconnect to a single 
POI under a single interconnection agreement and both the generator and load 
would be parties to the agreement. 
2. 
Develop new transparent procedures for co-location customers (load and generators) 
to request to interconnect via the PJM Interconnection Queue Study Process, 
including for existing generators that wish to interconnect new end-use load 
customers.  The procedures and interconnection reliability studies would cover all 
potential modes of operation. 
3. 
Clearly define the terms and conditions of the Co-location Arrangement, including 
the right to make retail sales and cost responsibilities associated with serving the 
end-use load that is on par with serving network load that is front-of-the-meter. 
An alternative option would be a three-party agreement between the co-located 
generator, Interconnecting transmission owner and PJM, where the co-location generator will 
serve end-use load.   
Under either a three- or four-party agreement, the co-located generator would be able 
to connect to the grid, make wholesale sales to network load or point-to-point load customers, 
and make retail sales to its directly connected customers, subject to any applicable state tariff 
governing such retail sales.  The generator would be responsible for paying for transmission 
service commensurate with the maximum amount of load that it seeks to supply.  If the new 
co-located load and generation are appropriately sized to minimize new power flows on the 
grid, such a configuration would provide the least impact to the grid and therefore likely a 
candidate for an expedited study process.    
D. The Need for a Co-Location “Safety Valve” to Ensure System Reliability and 
Customer Affordability. 
 
The Show Cause Order asked the parties to “explain whether the existing Tariff rules 
are sufficient to ensure resource adequacy if increasing numbers of large existing generators

10 
 
choose to co-locate with load.”15  In our view, the mass migration of existing generators to a 
co-location configuration could absolutely threaten the reliability of the PJM grid and worsen 
the already dire affordability crisis faced by many PJM consumers.  To the best of our 
knowledge, none of the studies proposed by PJM or the Indicated Transmission Owners 
would evaluate resource adequacy considerations.   
The Commission should strongly consider a co-location “safety valve” that ensures 
that co-location does not drive PJM into shortage conditions.  As noted in NERC in 2023, 
“[d]riven by electrification, hydrogen production, data centers, crypto mining, and other 
computational and energy-intensive methods such as artificial intelligence (AI), new loads 
can emerge and grow faster than generation and transmission can be built.”16  And the 
situation has only grown more challenging since then.17  Requiring completion of the study 
process that addresses both transmission reliability and resource adequacy prior to energizing 
any new co-located load additions would help ensure system reliability and provide adequate 
time for markets to adjust to the changing supply-demand balance.   
As noted above, PJM had only 514 MW of excess capacity in the 2025/2026 delivery 
year.  Load is projected to grow substantially in 2026, with over 2,700 MW of new load 
growth now expected above levels projected in 2024.  There is no need to recount the litany 
of challenges that PJM has faced interconnecting new generators or the fact that its three-year 
forward auction is now effectively a prompt auction.  Nuclear generating units, for example, 
have been particularly attractive candidates for co-location.  Removing even a single nuclear 
generator from the capacity supply stack would, assuming current market trends hold, drive 
PJM into a resource adequacy shortfall.  PJM’s existing rules appear to have no effective 
 
15 Show Cause Order at p. 53.   
16 ERO Reliability Risk Priorities Report North American Electric Reliability Corporation, August 
2023 at p. 27 (emphasis added). 
17 See Statement PJM CEO to OPSI, “I feel more concerned today than I did two years ago about 
resource adequacy.  Load is growing much faster than we had projected then, which even back then 
was an eye-popping set of numbers.”  Available at:  
http://www.paenvironmentdigest.com/newsletter/default.asp?NewsletterArticleID=61689&SubjectID=
217.

11 
 
means of limiting these departures or staggering the departures until new replacement 
resources are identified and built.  The clogged interconnection queue and short capacity 
auction time horizon makes bringing replacement resources to market quickly would be near 
impossible under the current circumstances.   
The reality is that the existing rules, which treat new load as network load, create a 
significant lag between the time new service is requested and the time it is provided by the 
utility.  While this is obviously commercially challenging for data center customers, it does 
act as something of a “governor” on the rate at which load can grow.  If the Commission 
elects to significantly accelerate co-location opportunities, the speed at which the new load 
comes online may accelerate significantly.  In such circumstances, the Commission should 
consider whether it is necessary for PJM to strategically manage the rate at which co-location 
is allowed if necessary to ensure continued system reliability.   
A safety valve could also help ensure customer affordability, which has been 
extremely challenged in light of the significant increases in capacity market prices for the 
2025/2026 delivery year.  It is important to recognize that co-location has the potential to 
significantly increase both capacity and energy prices, as energy prices tend to increase when 
the amount of excess generation shrinks.  As noted above, nuclear units are particularly 
attractive co-location candidates, and the sudden removal of significant quantities of $0 
marginal cost generation could put significant upward pressure on Locational Marginal Prices.    
E. The Commission Should Address the Risk of Stranded Transmission 
Investment Associated with Co-Location. 
 
One significant consumer protection concern is how to manage the risk associated 
with transmission facilities to support new co-located or network load if that load does not 
materialize.  The transmission investment necessary to serve these new mega-loads is large 
and the payback period is long, and their electricity usage is highly uncertain.  Data center 
energy efficiency breakthroughs, better algorithm optimization, quantum computing, and the 
normal ups and downs of a new industry could all result in data centers using less – or more – 
energy than anticipated.  The stranded cost risk to consumers is real, particularly as virtually

12 
 
all of PJM’s proposed solutions continue to have data center-driven transmission investments 
collected through socialized cost allocation methodologies that are often spread costs over 
multiple jurisdictions.   
Indeed, individual states and utilities have begun implementing minimum contract 
terms, minimum service level requirements, and “take or pay” structures backed by financial 
security requirements, these measures only protect customers in the specific utility zone that 
is implementing those protections.  While long-term contracts, backed by postings of 
financial security may protect the customers of a single utility, such payments do little to 
protect customers in the rest of PJM.   
While the Commission is certainly not in the business of managing the economic 
development decisions of individual states, it should ensure that any PJM tariff changes 
account for the potential that data center load may not materialize and collaborate with its 
state partners to manage this risk.  The need for federal-state coordination is perfectly 
illustrated in an ongoing proceeding before the Ohio Public Utilities Commission.18  There, 
Ohio utilities are battling over whether data center customers should be required to enter 
long-term contracts before being allowed to connect to the grid.  Thus, the Commission 
should consider imposing comparable “take or pay” structures for new large loads triggering 
transmission upgrades and backed by financial security postings.   
F. The Commission Should Take PJM Up on its Offer to Develop a Non-Firm 
or Interruptible Tariff for Co-Located Resources.    
 
We recommend that the Commission explore the potential to develop a new level of 
transmission service that prioritizes connection of new flexible loads – both co-located and 
non-co-located.  Research has demonstrated that greater flexibility in operations could 
 
18 For a summary of the Ohio proceeding, see Yoon Kim, Connecting Data Centers to the Grid: An 
Innovative and Controversial Proposal from AEP Ohio, Sept. 2024, available at: 
 https://blogs.law.columbia.edu/climatechange/2024/09/12/guest-blog-connecting-data-centers-to-the-
grid-an-innovative-and-controversial-proposal-from-aep-ohio.

13 
 
alleviate the need for upgrades needed to enable connection of the new loads.19  As PJM notes 
in its description of Options 7, allowing flexible load to be dispatched in the real-time horizon 
“provides an opportunity for large load to integrate as a non-capacity backed load where it 
avoids capacity costs if willing to curtail to support reliability in advance of emergency 
conditions.”20  A new level of service might be beneficial to both conventionally connected 
large loads and co-located arrangements (and potentially benefit other customer types 
interested in activating demand-side flexibility).   
To implement a new non-firm or interruptible type of service, consideration would 
have to address the nature of the service, how such service would be compliant with NERC 
mandatory reliability standards, address operational control mechanisms and establish an 
appropriate rate for the service.  Non-firm or interruptible service may not be desirable for all 
new large load customers, but its availability to those willing to operate more flexibly can 
yield benefits to all users connected to the grid and should be prioritized.21 
G. The Commission Should Clarify the Regulatory Obligations of Generators 
Serving On-Site Load.  
 
As stated by PJM, its preference for designating load as network load in-front-of-the-
meter is for multiple reasons, including reduced operating complexity, reduced dependence 
on protective schemes that can mis-operate, more reliable service, enhanced ability to manage 
load curtailment, greater access to demand response and more comprehensive holistic 
planning.22  This preference is an acknowledgement of the importance of having adequate 
visibility of the system conditions such that PJM can direct the reliable operation of the grid. 
This can be assured when all load connections are subject to the same reliability standards. 
For load that is served by a utility that is subject to the Consolidate Transmission Owner’s 
 
19 Norris, T. H., T. Profeta, D. Patino-Echeverri, and A. Cowie-Haskell. 2025. Rethinking Load Growth: 
Assessing the Potential for Integration of Large Flexible Loads in US Power Systems. NI R 25-01. 
Durham, NC: Nicholas Institute for Energy, Environment & Sustainability, Duke University. 
20 Answer of PJM Interconnection to Show Cause Order, at Appendix A.   
 
22 PJM Interconnection LLC Answer at Page 38.

14 
 
Agreement (“CTOA”), each connection to a non-party is governed by Article 4.10 which 
requires that the utility enter into an agreement that ensures compliance with applicable 
standards and Good Utility Practice.23  This provision ensures that not only does each PJM 
Transmission Owner maintain its systems reliably, but also any connections to other systems, 
including load customers and other transmission systems as well.  When a load is directly 
connected to another customer’s facilities without being subject to the same standards, the 
connection potentially exposes the grid to additional risks.  For this reason, it is recommended 
that at a minimum, any connection to a system not subject to the CTOA, be subject to 
comparable provisions be incorporated into any co-location agreement.  
The importance of this requirement cannot be overstated.  The growth in hyperscale 
sized loads that may have a demand that is on par with a typical nuclear plant presents new 
challenges for operations that as an industry we are only beginning to fully grasp.  Two 
system events highlight the risks that these large loads introduce to the power grid.  One 
example was an event cited by NERC in its comments at the FERC Technical Conference on 
co-located large loads.  NERC explained how a single line to ground fault on a 138 kV line 
resulted in a momentary voltage drop that triggered the automatic separation of approximately 
1500 MW of data center load.24  ERCOT has experienced similar events where data center 
load exhibits voltage-sensitive behavior that is resulting in unexpected reduction in 
consumption.    
We are years from fully assessing the risks posed by these large data center loads and 
establishing reliability requirements and industry best practices to mitigate these risks. While 
 
23 See PJM Consolidated Transmission Owners Agreement, Article 4.10 Connections with Non-Parties.  
“No Party shall permit its Transmission Facilities or distribution facilities to be connected with the 
facilities of any entity which is not a Party without an interconnection agreement that contains 
provisions for the safe and reliable operation of each interconnection in accordance with Good Utility 
Practice, and principles, guidelines and standards of the Applicable Regional Reliability Council and 
NERC or comparable requirements of an applicable retail tariff or agreement approved by appropriate 
regulatory authority.” 
24  Howard Gugel. Statement of the North American Electric Reliability Corporation. 
Technical Conference on Large Loads Co-Located at Generating Facilities Docket No. AD24-11- 
000 November 1, 2024 at Page 2.

15 
 
we are years away, it is imperative that RTOs have the authority to require any necessary 
updates to the interconnections that may be required to maintain safe and reliable operation of 
the grid.  This requires that any connection is subject to an agreement with the appropriate 
terms and authority of the RTO to enforce it.  The current pro forma interconnection 
agreements do not contain sufficient protections and should, at a minimum, be updated 
accordingly if it is to be used for connecting co-located large loads. 
H.  The Commission Should Ensure that any Proposed Changes go Through a 
Thorough Stakeholder Vetting.   
 
The Commission should ensure that any new tariff process arising out of this Show 
Cause Order be subject to further development in an open stakeholder forum.  There is ample 
evidence of prior attempts by customers to effectuate rules outside the stakeholder process 
and attempt to implement new business models not defined in the PJM rules.  Invariably, PJM 
rejected such attempts and worked with members to convene a stakeholder process to 
determine if tariff changes were warranted, and if so, what those tariff changes and 
accompanying manuals should be.25  PJM and FERC should again reject implementing new 
rules for customers without allowing for an open stakeholder process to vet such efforts. 
IV. 
Conclusion 
The current PJM Tariff process for connecting network load or point-to-point load is 
just and reasonable as it currently exists.  The well-published concerns about inadequate 
resource additions to meet the projected load, however, warrant active FERC and PJM efforts 
to actively manage the amount of co-location load coming onto the system, the rate of such 
additions, and the protection of consumers from the risks that the load does not materialize as 
expected.  Data centers are being built within 2-3 years, but the lead time for new natural gas 
 
25 In April 20219 PJM initiated a stakeholder process to “[e]xplore alternatives, if any, in two phases to 
address the challenges with interconnecting merchant transmission such that the project may be eligible 
for rights that can be used for interconnection of future offshore generation” in response to a customer 
seeking to implement a new business model.  Another example is the High Voltage Direct Current 
Senior Task Force to “...to explore the possibility of participation of HVDC converters in PJM’s 
capacity market, including their technical capabilities, existing tariff and manual provisions and hurdles 
to participation, as well as potential tariff changes needed to enable such participation.”  PJM has a 
well-established protocol where members can identify a problem and request endorsement of an issue 
charge to address a need.

generators is on the order of 5 years or more.  While co-location may offer advantages that 
can ultimately be beneficial to all users, it should not distract from PJM’s active management 
of co-location arrangements.    
Should FERC make that determination that co-location should be permitted in the 
PJM footprint, it should direct PJM to convene an open stakeholder process to develop the 
rules to do so.  FERC should provide clear principles for PJM and others in developing tariff 
revisions.  FERC should establish a timeframe that would allow for robust stakeholder 
engagement to develop tariff revisions that can fairly balance the interests of all grid 
customers and consumers who rely on cost-effective and efficient system planning and 
operations.
